lines.speaker: M
lines.say: I went to school here, 1997 to 2001. I've walked Court Street hundreds of times. I bought all the beer, buggied all the burritos, and cheered the Bobcats. I walked Mulberry Street every week, and there was no sign. I called myself anti-racist then, and I still do. And I never once heard the name Christopher Davis. This film is about how a town forgets, and how even the people who think they're paying attention never get told.

lines.speaker: CLIP
lines.caption: Ohio at Ohio State, September 1999. Broadcast footage via Southwest Ohio Sports Archive on YouTube, used under fair use for commentary.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That's my Bobcats, fall 1999. I was a junior. I knew the fight song, I knew Peden Stadium, and I knew every bar on Court Street. What I didn't know was a name.
lines.caption: That's my Bobcats, fall 1999. I was a junior. I knew the fight song, I knew Peden Stadium, and I knew every bar on Court Street. What I didn't know was a name.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Now, I grew up on Athens being the good guys. Underground Railroad town. Folks hid people in their cellars. That's what my granddad told me, anyway.
lines.caption: Now, I grew up on Athens being the good guys. Underground Railroad town. Folks hid people in their cellars. That's what my granddad told me, anyway.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He's not wrong about the pride. Athens does remember itself as a haven. But outside Baker University Center stands a dark blue marker from the Equal Justice Initiative. E J I has documented at least fifteen racial terror lynchings in Ohio. One of them happened a few hundred feet from where students buy their textbooks.
lines.caption: He's not wrong about the pride. Athens does remember itself as a haven. But outside Baker University Center stands a dark blue marker from the Equal Justice Initiative. EJI has documented at least fifteen racial terror lynchings in Ohio. One of them happened a few hundred feet from where students buy their textbooks.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Here? In Athens? I figured that sort of thing was a Southern story.
lines.caption: Here? In Athens? I figured that sort of thing was a Southern story.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: Ray, I've got the 1880 census open. Lee Township, Athens County. Christopher C. Davis, twenty-four, farm laborer near Albany. Wife Kenziah. Two small children, Robertie and Silas. That's an Ohio family.
lines.caption: Ray, I've got the 1880 census open. Lee Township, Athens County. Christopher C. Davis, twenty-four, farm laborer near Albany. Wife Kenziah. Two small children, Robertie and Silas. That's an Ohio family.
lines.visual: card:1880 U.S. Census|Lee Township, Athens County · archive scan to come

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In late October 1881, a white neighbor, Lucinda Luckey, said Davis had tried to assault her. She said she saw him by dim lantern light. Davis said he was innocent. A neighbor gave him an alibi, and local papers spoke for his character.
lines.caption: In late October 1881, a white neighbor, Lucinda Luckey, said Davis had tried to assault her. She said she saw him by dim lantern light. Davis said he was innocent. A neighbor gave him an alibi, and local papers spoke for his character.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Well, there was a trial, though. The law handled it.
lines.caption: Well, there was a trial, though. The law handled it.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: The sheriff knew better than that. He moved Davis fifty miles away to Chillicothe for his own safety. They brought him back on November twentieth for trial. He never got one.
lines.caption: The sheriff knew better than that. He moved Davis fifty miles away to Chillicothe for his own safety. They brought him back on November twentieth for trial. He never got one.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: On the night of November twenty-first, 1881, a mob of white men broke into the Athens County jail. They dragged Christopher Davis to the South Bridge over the Hocking River, and they hanged him.
lines.caption: On the night of November twenty-first, 1881, a mob of white men broke into the Athens County jail. They dragged Christopher Davis to the South Bridge over the Hocking River, and they hanged him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: It did not end at the river. Davis was buried at West State Street Cemetery. Grave robbers dug him up without his family's consent and shipped his body to Starling Medical College in Columbus, to be cut apart for anatomy class.
lines.caption: It did not end at the river. Davis was buried at West State Street Cemetery. Grave robbers dug him up without his family's consent and shipped his body to Starling Medical College in Columbus, to be cut apart for anatomy class.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: And in 1882 a grand jury sat. Not one indictment.
lines.caption: And in 1882 a grand jury sat. Not one indictment.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Nobody? Not one name?
lines.caption: Nobody? Not one name?

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: Not one.
lines.caption: Not one.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: For well over a century, that was the official record: silence. It took O U graduate student Jordan Zdinak and alumna Jessica Cyders to dig it back up. Their research led to the soil ceremony at the bridge in 2019 and the marker on Mulberry Street in 2020.
lines.caption: For well over a century, that was the official record: silence. It took OU graduate student Jordan Zdinak and alumna Jessica Cyders to dig it back up. Their research led to the soil ceremony at the bridge in 2019 and the marker on Mulberry Street in 2020.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: My granddad never told me that one.
lines.caption: My granddad never told me that one.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: No. Most granddads didn't. Nobody told me either. When I was an undergrad, that marker didn't exist yet. Davis was killed a short walk from where I went to class, and I never knew.
lines.caption: No. Most granddads didn't. Nobody told me either. When I was an undergrad, that marker didn't exist yet. Davis was killed a short walk from where I went to class, and I never knew.

lines.speaker: CHAP
lines.visual: card:Act II|Trading the mob for bureaucracy, 1923 to 1974

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Alright, but that was 1881. By the 1900s, the university was a different animal. College town. Open doors.
lines.caption: Alright, but that was 1881. By the 1900s, the university was a different animal. College town. Open doors.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The doors were open the way a ledger is open: on paper, and only on the right page. In 1923 the Ohio University trustees adopted a rule barring out-of-state students who couldn't attend their own home state's public universities. That described almost exactly one group: Black students from the Jim Crow South.
lines.caption: The doors were open the way a ledger is open: on paper, and only on the right page. In 1923 the Ohio University trustees adopted a rule barring out-of-state students who couldn't attend their own home state's public universities. That described almost exactly one group: Black students from the Jim Crow South.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: The policy never says Black. It doesn't have to. Same with the College of Education, which quietly stopped placing Black student teachers in local classrooms.
lines.caption: The policy never says Black. It doesn't have to. Same with the College of Education, which quietly stopped placing Black student teachers in local classrooms.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Huh. So nobody had to say it out loud.
lines.caption: Huh. So nobody had to say it out loud.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: That's the trick, Ray. Write it down plain enough and nobody ever has to say it out loud.
lines.caption: That's the trick, Ray. Write it down plain enough and nobody ever has to say it out loud.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: And the old way hadn't gone anywhere. That same spring, the Klan paper The Fiery Cross reported on a large Klan funeral in Glouster and recruiting drives across Athens County.
lines.caption: And the old way hadn't gone anywhere. That same spring, the Klan paper The Fiery Cross reported on a large Klan funeral in Glouster and recruiting drives across Athens County.
lines.visual: card:The Fiery Cross|May 11, 1923 · archive scan to come

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Glouster? My cousin's from Glouster.
lines.caption: Glouster? My cousin's from Glouster.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: Then your cousin's town was in the paper.
lines.caption: Then your cousin's town was in the paper.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: By mid-century, local historians describe Athens as a very unwelcoming town to African Americans. Black students were refused service in Court Street restaurants and steered to off-campus housing on the west side.
lines.caption: By mid-century, local historians describe Athens as a very unwelcoming town to African Americans. Black students were refused service in Court Street restaurants and steered to off-campus housing on the west side.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Now, Court Street's where everybody goes.
lines.caption: Now, Court Street's where everybody goes.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: Everybody who got served.
lines.caption: Everybody who got served.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: Members of all races are admitted to the University and to the use of its facilities on an equal basis. ... However, it is believed that Administrators should make every reasonable effort to achieve the greatest degree of happiness and satisfaction to the greatest number of people.
lines.caption: Members of all races are admitted to the University and to the use of its facilities on an equal basis. ... However, it is believed that Administrators should make every reasonable effort to achieve the greatest degree of happiness and satisfaction to the greatest number of people.
lines.visual: card:Ohio University housing policy, 1944|“the greatest number of people” · OU Archives

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Well, that sounds fair enough. Equal basis.
lines.caption: Well, that sounds fair enough. Equal basis.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: Read the next sentence, Ray. The greatest number of people meant the white students. Black students would board in private homes in town. And if enough of them came, the policy said, perhaps a cottage could be set aside for them.
lines.caption: Read the next sentence, Ray. The greatest number of people meant the white students. Black students would board in private homes in town. And if enough of them came, the policy said, perhaps a cottage could be set aside for them.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: President Walter Sylvester Gamertsfelder's administration approved that policy in 1944. Even after Black students moved into the same dorms, the housing form kept a race preference checklist. Housing wasn't officially desegregated until 1963.
lines.caption: President Walter Sylvester Gamertsfelder's administration approved that policy in 1944. Even after Black students moved into the same dorms, the housing form kept a race preference checklist. Housing wasn't officially desegregated until 1963.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Then there's the Berry. In 1892, Edward and Mattie Berry, Black entrepreneurs, opened a hotel on North Court Street. By every account it was the finest in town, and it welcomed everyone. Ohio University bought it in 1961. In 1974 the university knocked it down for a parking lot.
lines.caption: Then there's the Berry. In 1892, Edward and Mattie Berry, Black entrepreneurs, opened a hotel on North Court Street. By every account it was the finest in town, and it welcomed everyone. Ohio University bought it in 1961. In 1974 the university knocked it down for a parking lot.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Well, a town needs parking.
lines.caption: Well, a town needs parking.

lines.speaker: K
lines.say: The lot was never built, Ray. It's Hangover Easy now. The out of place streetcar diner.
lines.caption: The lot was never built, Ray. It's Hangover Easy now. The out of place streetcar diner.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Then what'd they tear it down for?
lines.caption: Then what'd they tear it down for?

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: That's the question this whole film keeps asking.
lines.caption: That's the question this whole film keeps asking.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Okay. I'll grant you the old days. But that's history. Nobody's tearing anything down now. We put up a marker, didn't we?
lines.caption: Okay. I'll grant you the old days. But that's history. Nobody's tearing anything down now. We put up a marker, didn't we?

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: We did, Ray. In 2020. Want to see what happened five years later?
lines.caption: We did, Ray. In 2020. Want to see what happened five years later?

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: I'm guessing I don't.
lines.caption: I'm guessing I don't.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: If history teaches anything, it's that institutions rarely need force to give in. They need a political shift and an instinct for self-preservation. In 2025 that played out across Ohio fast.
lines.caption: If history teaches anything, it's that institutions rarely need force to give in. They need a political shift and an instinct for self-preservation. In 2025 that played out across Ohio fast.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: March twenty-eighth, 2025. Governor Mike DeWine signs Senate Bill 1, the Advance Ohio Higher Education Act. It bans D E I offices at public universities. It takes effect June twenty-seventh.
lines.caption: March twenty-eighth, 2025. Governor Mike DeWine signs Senate Bill 1, the Advance Ohio Higher Education Act. It bans DEI offices at public universities. It takes effect June twenty-seventh.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: So the university had till summer.
lines.caption: So the university had till summer.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: It had till summer. It didn't use it. That spring, Ohio University shut its Division of Diversity and Inclusion. The Multicultural Center, the Pride Center and the Women's Center inside Baker University Center were closed and their signs came down.
lines.caption: It had till summer. It didn't use it. That spring, Ohio University shut its Division of Diversity and Inclusion. The Multicultural Center, the Pride Center and the Women's Center inside Baker University Center were closed and their signs came down.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In April, O U President Lori Stewart Gonzalez emailed administrators. Staff were told, quote, not to look for ways to recreate the same approaches under a different name.
lines.caption: In April, OU President Lori Stewart Gonzalez emailed administrators. Staff were told, quote, not to look for ways to recreate the same approaches under a different name.
lines.visual: card:“not to look for ways to recreate the same approaches under a different name”|OU President Lori Stewart Gonzalez, April 2025 · via Signal Ohio

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Under a different name. Huh. That's the 1923 trick backwards, isn't it? Back then you didn't say the word. Now you can't say the word.
lines.caption: Under a different name. Huh. That's the 1923 trick backwards, isn't it? Back then you didn't say the word. Now you can't say the word.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: Now you're doing my job, Ray.
lines.caption: Now you're doing my job, Ray.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: O U was not alone. Across the state and the country, schools ran a race of anticipatory obedience.
lines.caption: OU was not alone. Across the state and the country, schools ran a race of anticipatory obedience.
lines.visual: card:Falling in line|Ohio and beyond, 2025 · map graphic to come

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: Ohio State closed its Office of Diversity and Inclusion and its Center for Belonging and Social Change in February 2025, before Senate Bill 1 was even law. Cincinnati and Case Western cut D E I staff and programs by March.
lines.caption: Ohio State closed its Office of Diversity and Inclusion and its Center for Belonging and Social Change in February 2025, before Senate Bill 1 was even law. Cincinnati and Case Western cut DEI staff and programs by March.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: In April, the University of Toledo announced it would drop undergraduate majors, including Africana Studies and Women's and Gender Studies.
lines.caption: In April, the University of Toledo announced it would drop undergraduate majors, including Africana Studies and Women's and Gender Studies.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Now hold on. Toledo's a MAC school. That's family.
lines.caption: Now hold on. Toledo's a MAC school. That's family.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: Family's in the record too, Ray.
lines.caption: Family's in the record too, Ray.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: Out of state: Michigan closed its central D E I office. Nebraska Omaha closed its diversity center, pointing to federal funding threats. Kentucky closed its Office for Institutional Diversity and canceled its identity-based graduation celebrations.
lines.caption: Out of state: Michigan closed its central DEI office. Nebraska Omaha closed its diversity center, pointing to federal funding threats. Kentucky closed its Office for Institutional Diversity and canceled its identity-based graduation celebrations.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Sara Kilpatrick of the Ohio Conference of the American Association of University Professors called it complying in advance. The University of Cincinnati's faculty senate chair, Steve Mockabee, said leaders were bending over backwards to over-comply.
lines.caption: Sara Kilpatrick of the Ohio Conference of the American Association of University Professors called it complying in advance. The University of Cincinnati's faculty senate chair, Steve Mockabee, said leaders were bending over backwards to over-comply.
lines.visual: card:“complying in advance”|Sara Kilpatrick, Ohio Conference AAUP

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Okay, but a map? That's just a map. Who cares what a phone calls a body of water?
lines.caption: Okay, but a map? That's just a map. Who cares what a phone calls a body of water?
lines.visual: card:The Gulf|January to February 2025 · screen recording to come

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: January twentieth, 2025. Executive Order 14172, Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness. It tells federal agencies to call the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. That's federal agencies, Ray. Not companies.
lines.caption: January twentieth, 2025. Executive Order 14172, Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness. It tells federal agencies to call the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. That's federal agencies, Ray. Not companies.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Legal scholars were clear: the order bound the federal government, not private businesses. The name Gulf of Mexico had been in use for more than four centuries. Google didn't have to do a thing.
lines.caption: Legal scholars were clear: the order bound the federal government, not private businesses. The name Gulf of Mexico had been in use for more than four centuries. Google didn't have to do a thing.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: January twenty-eighth, Google says it'll follow the federal database. February tenth, Google Maps shows Gulf of America to everyone in the United States. People flood the listing with angry reviews, and Google turns reviews off.
lines.caption: January twenty-eighth, Google says it'll follow the federal database. February tenth, Google Maps shows Gulf of America to everyone in the United States. People flood the listing with angry reviews, and Google turns reviews off.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: I'll say it plainly, as my opinion: Google went full chicken.
lines.caption: I'll say it plainly, as my opinion: Google went full chicken.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: And five days before the map changed, on February fifth, Google ended its diversity hiring targets.
lines.caption: And five days before the map changed, on February fifth, Google ended its diversity hiring targets.
lines.visual: card:February 5, 2025|Google ends its diversity hiring targets

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: Nobody made 'em.
lines.caption: Nobody made 'em.

lines.speaker: S
lines.say: Nobody made any of them, Ray. That's the story.
lines.caption: Nobody made any of them, Ray. That's the story.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: You know what gets me? I always figured the bad part of history was the loud part. The rope. The torches.
lines.caption: You know what gets me? I always figured the bad part of history was the loud part. The rope. The torches.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: From the South Bridge in 1881 to the trustees' rule of 1923, the wrecking crews of 1974 and the boardrooms of 2025, the machinery hasn't changed much.
lines.caption: From the South Bridge in 1881 to the trustees' rule of 1923, the wrecking crews of 1974 and the boardrooms of 2025, the machinery hasn't changed much.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Exclusion and erasure don't always come with a rope or a torch. Now they come as a P D F memo, a locked door in a student center, a new label on a map.
lines.caption: Exclusion and erasure don't always come with a rope or a torch. Now they come as a PDF memo, a locked door in a student center, a new label on a map.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: When universities and tech giants bend the knee before anyone asks, erasure needs no mob. It needs only compliance.
lines.caption: When universities and tech giants bend the knee before anyone asks, erasure needs no mob. It needs only compliance.

lines.speaker: R
lines.say: I'm gonna go read that sign on Mulberry Street.
lines.caption: I'm gonna go read that sign on Mulberry Street.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Me too, Ray. Twenty-five years late.
lines.caption: Me too, Ray. Twenty-five years late.
